newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Clinton signals NATO race by Poland, Hungary, Czechs.
newsitem.headline: Clinton signals NATO race by Poland, Hungary, Czechs.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, fixing a 1999 target date for admitting new members to NATO, has launched a furious race by the alliance's former communist foes desperate to join at the first attempt.

Clinton did not name countries but NATO military circles say Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic lead the field for the biggest transformation of Europe's political and security map since the end of communism.

His campaign speech in Detroit on Tuesday, carefully worded to assure countries of Central and Eastern Europe the "door would stay open", will intensify lobbying campaigns, defence analysts and Western diplomats say.
"There will be a huge push by some countries just outside at the moment, coupled with more and more attention on what to offer those countries which do not make it," said one NATO official.
The American leader did not set a date for a summit next year to invite countries to open membership negotiations.
Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia all harbour hopes they can be in the first wave. Behind them, the Baltic states -- desperate to cement their divorce from Moscow -- are watching anxiously.
Bratislava, virtually ruled out by the West for its failure to make progress on democratic reforms, has warned that leaving it out could increase tensions in the region.
Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik recently said security guarantees for Slovakia's neighbours would leave it in "a grey zone" which was the same as no security at all.
Diplomats say Romania presents another problem altogether.

"Bucharest has made tremendous progress on the military front and fulfills many membership conditions (but)... no-body thinks it is sufficently economically-developed to be a serious contender," said one alliance military official.

Slovenia has also recently emerged as a possible candidate for membership with NATO countries apparently evenly divided between the advantages and disadvantages of taking in the former Yugoslav republic.

"It could be seen as a reward for keeping out of the conflict and be seen as spreading stability, on the other hand it will infuriate Croatia and bring a spate of demands for membership from the others," added the military official.
British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo said on Wednesday enlargement was an on-going process, but accepted there would be a huge push by applicant states in coming months.

"There is much gnashing of teeth by those who fear they will not be among the first new members, and by those who would rather not see enlargement happen," he said in a speech at a defence institute in Belgium.
Russia, apparently accepting it cannot stop alliance expansion, is expected to campaign to limit it to a handful of countries -- a prospect viewed with alarm by the Baltic states.
"The countries most in need of protection are those least likely to get any," quipped one senior alliance ambassador.
NATO diplomats say that whatever happens countries who do not make it in the first round will be expecting something to cushion the blow.
"They want to be mentioned by name as likely future members and in the interim they want much closer links," said another official.

Anticipating that request, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe General George Joulwan said on Tuesday cooperation programmes, such as Partnership for Peace (PFP), would go on, despite the 1999 target date.
"No matter what, PFP must continue to develop the way ahead," he told a news conference in Hungary.
